questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which finding after head trauma most strongly requires immediate reassessment and escalation?
choices: A patient asking what time it is once
A falling motor response and new unequal pupils
Mild fatigue after a poor night's sleep with an unchanged examination
An unchanged scar from prior surgery
questions.explanation: A new motor decline and pupillary asymmetry can indicate evolving intracranial injury. Repeat the focused neurologic assessment and promptly alert the trauma or neurosurgical team.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: An older adult on apixaban falls and has no obvious injury. What medication detail should the RN communicate during the head-injury evaluation?
choices: The exact anticoagulant and time of the last dose
Only the medication's tablet color
That anticoagulation always proves there is an intracranial bleed
That the medication can be ignored if the patient is talking
questions.explanation: Anticoagulant exposure affects imaging and bleeding-risk decisions. The treating clinician needs the exact drug and last dose; an initially normal conversation does not exclude later deterioration.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A patient with TBI becomes hypoxemic and hypotensive. Which priority best limits secondary brain injury?
choices: Wait for a new CT before addressing oxygenation or perfusion
Focus only on the original impact site
Promptly support airway, oxygenation, and circulation while evaluating the cause
Assume low blood pressure improves cerebral blood flow
questions.explanation: Hypoxemia and hypotension are preventable secondary insults after TBI. Immediate airway and perfusion support, while identifying trauma-related causes, protects the injured brain.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: What should the RN do when a patient becomes more confused several hours after an initially reassuring head CT?
choices: Discharge because the first image was normal
Ignore the change unless fever develops
Give an unsupervised sedative and defer neurologic checks
Repeat and document the neurologic assessment and urgently notify the treating team
questions.explanation: Intracranial findings and symptoms can evolve after initial assessment. New confusion requires a fresh neurologic examination and urgent clinical review, not reassurance from an earlier scan.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: In a severe TBI patient with ordered ICP and CPP monitoring, which statement is accurate?
choices: CPP is calculated by adding ICP to mean arterial pressure
CPP equals mean arterial pressure minus ICP, and trends are interpreted with the clinical examination
A single normal CPP eliminates the need for neurologic reassessment
The RN should change the ICP treatment target without an order
questions.explanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is MAP minus ICP. The RN follows individualized targets and monitors trends together with the neurologic examination and the patient's overall condition.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Why is prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation not routinely used in severe TBI?
choices: It can reduce cerebral blood flow and worsen ischemia
It always raises carbon dioxide to dangerous levels
It replaces the need for airway protection
It reliably prevents every post-traumatic seizure
questions.explanation: Routine prolonged hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide and may constrict cerebral vessels, reducing blood flow to already vulnerable tissue. Ventilation changes require a specialist plan.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which set of observations is most useful for trending a head-injury neurologic examination?
choices: Only one total GCS score at admission
Only the patient's pain score
Serial GCS components, pupils, limb movement, speech, behavior, and vital signs
Only the result of the first CT scan
questions.explanation: Repeated, component-level GCS and focused neurologic findings reveal subtle deterioration. Pupils, motor symmetry, behavior, and vital-sign changes add context that one number cannot provide.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which nursing action is appropriate for an external ventricular drain in a severe TBI patient?
choices: Change the drainage height independently whenever ICP rises
Leave the drain open during every transport regardless of protocol
Flush the catheter routinely without an order
Follow prescribed leveling, drainage, clamping, and infection-prevention procedures
questions.explanation: EVD management is protocol- and order-dependent. Incorrect leveling or drainage can cause harm, so the RN follows the prescribed plan and reports abnormal output or neurologic change.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which discharge teaching is most appropriate after a clinician clears an adult with a mild TBI for home care?
choices: Remain in strict bed rest for several weeks despite improving symptoms
Use brief initial rest, then gradually resume light activity and seek urgent care for worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, or seizure
Return immediately to contact sports even if symptoms remain
Ignore symptoms that worsen after activity
questions.explanation: CDC guidance supports brief rest followed by gradual symptom-guided activity. Written return precautions and home supervision help detect delayed deterioration or persistent symptoms.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: What is the best evidence that acute TBI care is stabilizing?
choices: An unchanged or improving neurologic examination with adequate oxygenation and perfusion
A single normal oxygen-saturation reading despite falling GCS
A headache that disappears after sedation without reassessment
One CT scan with no follow-up examination
questions.explanation: Stable neurologic trends plus adequate oxygenation and perfusion indicate that immediate priorities are being met. One isolated reading or symptom is not enough to judge recovery.
